The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear operator of infinite rank, viewed as an inverse model with exact datum $Kx$. Here compact means that the image of every bounded subset has compact closure. Write $N(K)=\{x\in X:Kx=0\}$ and $H_0=\overline{\operatorname{ran}K}$. Fix a positive singular system $(s_j,v_j,u_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ for $K$, where $\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$, $s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots>0$, $s_j\to0$, $Kv_j=s_ju_j$, $(v_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $N(K)^\perp$, and $(u_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $H_0$. A complete orthonormal basis is an orthonormal family whose closed linear span is the whole indicated subspace. These are the compact SVD conventions; in particular, this model concerns minimum-norm representatives in $N(K)^\perp$ and does not estimate a kernel component.

For a truth $x\in N(K)^\perp$, let $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$. The complete-basis coefficient map identifies $N(K)^\perp$ bijectively and isometrically with $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, so every $\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ is a model parameter. For $\epsilon>0$, take the functional white-noise experiment on the separable Hilbert space $H_0$ with observations $Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_Y+\epsilon W(g)$, where $W$ is centered, has covariance $\mathbb E[W(g)W(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_Y$, and has independent standard-normal values on every finite orthonormal tuple. The countable complete basis makes $H_0$ separable. Define $\xi_j=W(u_j)$ and $Z_j=Y_x(u_j)/s_j$. The sequence sample space is $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ with the product Borel sigma-algebra, meaning the sigma-algebra generated by its coordinate projections. The coordinate law is the pushforward of the functional experiment under $y\mapsto(y(u_j)/s_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$; this map is measurable because each coordinate is a cylinder evaluation followed by scalar multiplication. The compact SVD expansion gives $\langle Kx,u_j\rangle_Y=s_j\theta_j$, and the positive-noise white-noise coordinate theorem gives the independent standard-normal coordinates $\xi_j$. Hence the normalized coordinates satisfy $Z_j=\theta_j+\epsilon s_j^{-1}\xi_j,\qquad j\in\mathbb N.$

For the zero-noise boundary $\epsilon=0$, define the sequence experiment separately by the point mass at $\theta$, so $Z_j=\theta_j$. This boundary is not an instance of the positive-noise functional experiment.

Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, where separable means having a countable dense subset, and let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space. A real isonormal Gaussian process on $H$ is a family $Z(g)$ of real random variables with finite second moments, indexed by $g\in H$, such that $g\mapsto[Z(g)]$ is linear into $L^2(\mathbb P)$, $\mathbb E Z(g)=0$, and $\mathbb E[Z(g)Z(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_H$. It is also required that for every finite orthonormal tuple $(e_1,\ldots,e_m)$ the variables $Z(e_1),\ldots,Z(e_m)$ are independent and each has density $\varphi(t)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-t^2/2}$. For any finite list of vectors, expressing them in an orthonormal basis of their finite-dimensional span shows that their process values have the corresponding linear-image Gaussian law. Here $L^2(\mathbb P)$ identifies square-integrable random variables that agree almost surely. When $H\ne\{0\}$, all unit-vector marginals have the same law; write $N(a,\sigma^2)$ for the law of $a+\sigma Z(e)$ for any unit vector $e\in H$ and $\sigma\ge0$.

Let $X$ be a set, let $\Theta\subseteq X$ be a nonempty parameter set, let $K:X\to H$ be a signal map, and let $\epsilon>0$. For $x\in\Theta$ and $g\in H$, define the observation functional

$$Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_H+\epsilon Z(g).$$

The associated statistical inverse experiment has sample space $\mathbb R^H$ with the cylinder sigma-algebra generated by the evaluation maps $y\mapsto y(g)$, and its sampling law $P_x$ is the law of the random function $g\mapsto Y_x(g)$. Each sample is indexed by test functionals on $H$; it is not asserted to be a vector in $H$ or to have a continuous path. If $H=\{0\}$, linearity forces $Z(0)=0$ and the experiment is deterministic.

An **experiment** is a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a set $\Theta$ of
parameter labels, and a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of probability
measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ (Measurable spaces and measurable sets,
Probability measures and probability spaces). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.
If data under a parameter value are realized as a random element, its law is
the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
Law or distribution of a random element; it is a probability measure by
The law of a random element is a probability measure.

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra
on $\Theta$, no measurability condition on $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$, and no
common underlying probability space on which all observations must be realized.

A **measurable space** is a pair $(X,\mathcal A)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a
sigma-algebra $\mathcal A$ on $X$ (Sigma-algebras). The members of
$\mathcal A$ are the **measurable subsets** of $X$.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space (Topology on a set, open and closed sets, clopen sets, the closed-set axiomatisation, and the coarser/finer comparison). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by Nonempty intersections of sigma-algebras are sigma-algebras, so the generated sigma-algebra exists and is minimal.

Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
(Lebesgue outer measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, Assuming countable choice, Lebesgue outer measure is an outer measure that restricts to elementary volume
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of Carathéodory measurable sets.

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in Assuming countable choice, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra containing every elementary set and $\lambda_n$ is a complete measure extending elementary volume, which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

If $f:X\to Y$ is continuous between topological spaces, then
$f^{-1}[B]\in\mathcal B(X)$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(Y)$.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Then

$$\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\subseteq\; \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) :$$

every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ (The Borel sigma-algebra of a topological space) is Lebesgue
measurable (Lebesgue measurable sets, the family $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$, and the restricted set function $\lambda_n$). In
particular every open set, every closed set and every countable intersection of
open sets is Lebesgue measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ are measurable and $f+g$ is defined
   pointwise, then $f+g$ is measurable.
2. If $c\in\mathbb R$ and $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $cf$ is
   measurable.
3. If $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $f^+=\max\{f,0\}$,
   $f^-=\max\{-f,0\}$, and $|f|=f^++f^-$ are measurable.
4. If $E\in\mathcal A$ and $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $f\chi_E$ is measurable, where this function equals $f$ on $E$ and $0$
   off $E$ (in particular, $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ here).
5. If $(f_n)$ is a sequence of measurable functions $X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$,
   then $\inf_n f_n$ is measurable; if moreover $f_n\uparrow f$ pointwise, then
   $f$ is measurable.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment (Statistical experiments), let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable action space, meaning a set with
a specified sigma-algebra (Measurable spaces and measurable sets), and let
$L:\Theta\times\mathsf D\to[0,+\infty]$ be a loss function whose section
$a\mapsto L(\theta,a)$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable for each $\theta$. A
randomized decision rule is a probability kernel $\delta$ from the data space
to the action space (Randomized procedures as probability kernels). Its
**risk** at $\theta$ is the extended nonnegative number
$$R(\theta,\delta)=\int_{\mathcal X}\left(\int_{\mathsf D}L(\theta,a)\,\delta(x,da)\right)P_\theta(dx).$$
The inner integral is a measurable function of $x$, by
A randomized procedure has a measurable action law, so the outer nonnegative integral
is defined by Expectation of a nonnegative or integrable random variable.
A deterministic measurable rule is included by taking its point-mass action
kernel. No measurability on $\Theta$ is required for this definition.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]) and let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable **action space**: a set of available
actions equipped with a sigma-algebra of action events, hence a measurable
space ([[def-measurable-space]]). A **randomized procedure** (or
randomized decision rule) is a probability kernel $K$ from
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ to $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$, in the pointwise sense
of [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. Thus $K(x,\cdot)$ is a
probability measure on $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ for every $x\in\mathcal X$,
and $x\mapsto K(x,B)$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable for every $B\in\mathcal G$.
After observing $x$, the procedure assigns probability $K(x,B)$ to taking an
action in $B$. The kernel is specified without reference to the unknown
parameter. This definition imposes no measurable structure on $\Theta$. The
kernel is the specification of the procedure; no representation by a separate
random seed is asserted for arbitrary measurable action spaces.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be measurable
parameter and data spaces, with $\Theta$ nonempty, and let
$K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ be a probability kernel, writing
$P_\theta=K(\theta,\cdot)$ for the sampling law
([[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]]). Let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a nonempty measurable action space
([[def-measurable-space]]). Let $L:\Theta\times\mathsf D\to\overline{\mathbb R}$
be measurable from the product measurable space with sigma-algebra
$\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal G$ to the extended real line with its Borel
sigma-algebra, and assume $L(\theta,a)\geq0$ for all $(\theta,a)$
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]],
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]], [[def-extended-reals]],
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra-on-the-extended-real-line]]). A **prior** $\pi$ is a
probability measure on $\Theta$. The risk function $\theta\mapsto R(\theta,\delta)$ is measurable
under these hypotheses by kernel integration
([[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]],
[[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]]). The **Bayes risk** of
$\delta$ under $\pi$ is
$$r_\pi(\delta)=\int_\Theta R(\theta,\delta)\,\pi(d\theta)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Its **worst-case risk** is
$$R^*(\delta)=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}R(\theta,\delta)\in[0,+\infty],$$
and the **minimax value** is
$$V_{\rm mm}=\inf\{R^*(\delta):\delta\text{ is a measurable randomized rule from data to actions}\}\in[0,+\infty].$$
These suprema and infima are taken in the extended order on $\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]]); they exist by
[[lem-extended-reals-complete]]. The parameter set is nonempty and the rule
class is nonempty under the action-space hypothesis, so these are suprema and
infima of nonempty sets of nonnegative extended risks.
A rule is minimax if its worst-case risk equals this infimum. These definitions
make no assertion that a minimizer exists. Nonemptiness of $\mathsf D$ ensures
the rule class is nonempty: fixing any $a_0\in\mathsf D$ gives the constant
point-mass rule $x\mapsto\delta_{a_0}$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sinh x:=\frac{\exp x-\exp(-x)}2,\qquad\cosh x:=\frac{\exp x+\exp(-x)}2,$$
$$\tanh x:=\frac{\sinh x}{\cosh x},\qquad\operatorname{sech}x:=\frac1{\cosh x}.$$
For $x\ne0$, define
$$\coth x:=\frac{\cosh x}{\sinh x},\qquad\operatorname{csch}x:=\frac1{\sinh x}.$$

The positivity of $\exp$ makes $\cosh x>0$ for every $x$. If $x\ne0$, then
$x\ne-x$, so strict increase of $\exp$ makes $\exp x\ne\exp(-x)$; hence
$\sinh x\ne0$. Thus all four quotients above are defined on exactly their
stated domains ([[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]],
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]]).

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sinh(x+y)=\sinh x\cosh y+\cosh x\sinh y,\qquad\cosh(x+y)=\cosh x\cosh y+\sinh x\sinh y,$$
$$\cosh^2x-\sinh^2x=1,\qquad(\sinh x)'=\cosh x,\qquad(\cosh x)'=\sinh x.$$
Moreover $\sinh:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is odd, strictly increasing, and onto;
$\cosh:\mathbb R\to[1,\infty)$ is even and positive, and its restriction
to $[0,\infty)$ is strictly increasing and onto $[1,\infty)$; and
$\tanh:\mathbb R\to(-1,1)$ is strictly increasing and onto. On their declared domains,
$$(\tanh x)'=\operatorname{sech}^2x,\quad(\coth x)'=-\operatorname{csch}^2x,\quad(\operatorname{sech}x)'=-\operatorname{sech}x\tanh x,\quad(\operatorname{csch}x)'=-\operatorname{csch}x\coth x.$$

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in The exponential series converges absolutely for every real argument. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of The factorial $n!$ and the falling factorial $n^{\underline{k}}$, defined by recursion in $\mathbb{N}$, $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing), and powers and series are those of Integer powers $a^m$ and Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series.

This is a real power series centred at $0$ (A real power series about a centre, its interval of convergence, and its radius in $[0,+\infty]$). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

This is a real power series centred at $0$ (A real power series about a centre, its interval of convergence, and its radius in $[0,+\infty]$). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt\pi.$$

If $f$ has a possible singularity at $c\in(a,b)$, define
$$\int_a^b f:=\int_a^c f+\int_c^b f$$
only when the two one-sided improper integrals converge separately. Cancellation between divergent sides is not allowed.

Likewise, for any finite split point $s$, define
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f:=\int_{-\infty}^{s}f+\int_s^\infty f$$
only when both tails converge. More generally, an interval with several singular ends is split into finitely many one-ended pieces, each of which must converge separately. Independence of the permitted split point is a theorem, not part of this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $a\in\mathbb R$ and let
$f:[a,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be Riemann integrable on every compact interval
$[a,R]$ with $R>a$. If the improper Riemann integral
$$\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx$$
converges in the sense of [[def-improper-integral-at-infinity]], then $f$ is
Lebesgue integrable on $[a,\infty)$ and
$$\int_{[a,\infty)} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

(Axis-parallel rectangles in $\mathbb{R}^m$ and their volume). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of Half-open boxes in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and their volume, and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ (Assuming countable choice, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra containing every elementary set and $\lambda_n$ is a complete measure extending elementary volume).

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $E$ be measurable with $\mu(E)=0$.
Then
$$\int_E f\,d\mu=0.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. If $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ are measurable, then
$$\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu.$$

Let $I$ and $J$ be intervals, possibly open at finite or infinite singular ends, and let $\phi:I\to J$ be a monotone differentiable surjection. Assume $\phi'$ is locally Riemann integrable and the proper change-of-variable hypotheses hold on every compact truncation. If $f$ is locally Riemann integrable on $J$, then
$$\int_J f(x)\,dx\quad\text{and}\quad\int_I f(\phi(t))|\phi'(t)|\,dt$$
converge simultaneously and, when convergent, are equal. At several singular ends this assertion is applied separately to the corresponding ends; orientation is retained for decreasing parametrizations.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$) at which $g$ is differentiable
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of If $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \ne 0$ then $|f| > |L|/2$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; in particular if $L > 0$ then $f > L/2 > 0$ there applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
Carathéodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi$ is unique and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of Sums, scalar multiples, products, absolute values, maxima, minima and quotients with nonvanishing denominator of continuous functions are continuous, as are constants, the identity and every polynomial function.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point, Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

A complete orthonormal basis is an orthonormal family whose closed linear span is the whole indicated subspace. These are the compact SVD conventions; in particular, this model concerns minimum-norm representatives in $N(K)^\perp$ and does not estimate a kernel component.

For a truth $x\in N(K)^\perp$, let $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$. The complete-basis coefficient map identifies $N(K)^\perp$ bijectively and isometrically with $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, so every $\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ is a model parameter. For $\epsilon>0$, take the functional white-noise experiment on the separable Hilbert space $H_0$ with observations $Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_Y+\epsilon W(g)$, where $W$ is centered, has covariance $\mathbb E[W(g)W(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_Y$, and has independent standard-normal values on every finite orthonormal tuple. The countable complete basis makes $H_0$ separable. Define $\xi_j=W(u_j)$ and $Z_j=Y_x(u_j)/s_j$. The sequence sample space is $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ with the product Borel sigma-algebra, meaning the sigma-algebra generated by its coordinate projections. The coordinate law is the pushforward of the functional experiment under $y\mapsto(y(u_j)/s_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$; this map is measurable because each coordinate is a cylinder evaluation followed by scalar multiplication. The compact SVD expansion gives $\langle Kx,u_j\rangle_Y=s_j\theta_j$, and the positive-noise white-noise coordinate theorem gives the independent standard-normal coordinates $\xi_j$. Hence the normalized coordinates satisfy $Z_j=\theta_j+\epsilon s_j^{-1}\xi_j,\qquad j\in\mathbb N.$

exactly the positive singular values counted with multiplicity, which we write

   $(f_j)_{j\in J}$ in $\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}$, indexed by exactly $J$,
   with $|T|e_j=s_je_j$ and $f_j=s_j^{-1}Te_j$ for every $j\in J$;
2. for every $x\in H$ the series converges in norm and
   $$Tx=\sum_{j\in J}s_j\langle x,e_j\rangle f_j,$$
   and its finite partial sums
   $T_n:=\sum_{j\le n}s_j\langle\cdot,e_j\rangle f_j$ satisfy

   orthonormal systems: the systems carry exactly the index set $J$ of the

$$q(S)x:=q(0)P_0x+\sum_{t\in\Sigma}q(t)P_tx,$$

$$g_\lambda(t)=\frac1{t+\lambda},\qquad r_\lambda(t)=1-tg_\lambda(t)=\frac{\lambda}{t+\lambda}.$$
The Tikhonov solution for data $y_\delta\in Y$ is
$$x_\lambda^\delta=g_\lambda(S)A^*y_\delta =(A^*A+\lambda I_X)^{-1}A^*y_\delta.$$
Indeed, the spectral decomposition gives $S+\lambda I_X$ the multiplier
$t+\lambda$ on each $E_t$ and $\lambda$ on $\ker S$, so $g_\lambda(S)$ is

$$t^\nu|r_\alpha(t)|\le C_\nu\alpha^\nu \quad\text{for every }\alpha>0\text{ and }t\in\Sigma.$$

randomized decision rule is a probability kernel $\delta$ from the data space
to the action space (Randomized procedures as probability kernels). Its
**risk** at $\theta$ is the extended nonnegative number
$$R(\theta,\delta)=\int_{\mathcal X}\left(\int_{\mathsf D}L(\theta,a)\,\delta(x,da)\right)P_\theta(dx).$$
The inner integral is a measurable function of $x$, by
A randomized procedure has a measurable action law, so the outer nonnegative integral
is defined by Expectation of a nonnegative or integrable random variable.
A deterministic measurable rule is included by taking its point-mass action
kernel. No measurability on $\Theta$ is required for this definition.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]) and let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable **action space**: a set of available
actions equipped with a sigma-algebra of action events, hence a measurable
space ([[def-measurable-space]]). A **randomized procedure** (or
randomized decision rule) is a probability kernel $K$ from
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ to $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$, in the pointwise sense
of [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. Thus $K(x,\cdot)$ is a
probability measure on $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ for every $x\in\mathcal X$,
and $x\mapsto K(x,B)$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable for every $B\in\mathcal G$.
After observing $x$, the procedure assigns probability $K(x,B)$ to taking an
action in $B$. The kernel is specified without reference to the unknown
parameter. This definition imposes no measurable structure on $\Theta$. The
kernel is the specification of the procedure; no representation by a separate
random seed is asserted for arbitrary measurable action spaces.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be measurable
parameter and data spaces, with $\Theta$ nonempty, and let
$K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ be a probability kernel, writing
$P_\theta=K(\theta,\cdot)$ for the sampling law
([[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]]). Let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a nonempty measurable action space
([[def-measurable-space]]). Let $L:\Theta\times\mathsf D\to\overline{\mathbb R}$
be measurable from the product measurable space with sigma-algebra
$\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal G$ to the extended real line with its Borel
sigma-algebra, and assume $L(\theta,a)\geq0$ for all $(\theta,a)$
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]],
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]], [[def-extended-reals]],
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra-on-the-extended-real-line]]). A **prior** $\pi$ is a
probability measure on $\Theta$. The risk function $\theta\mapsto R(\theta,\delta)$ is measurable
under these hypotheses by kernel integration
([[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]],
[[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]]). The **Bayes risk** of
$\delta$ under $\pi$ is
$$r_\pi(\delta)=\int_\Theta R(\theta,\delta)\,\pi(d\theta)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Its **worst-case risk** is
$$R^*(\delta)=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}R(\theta,\delta)\in[0,+\infty],$$
and the **minimax value** is
$$V_{\rm mm}=\inf\{R^*(\delta):\delta\text{ is a measurable randomized rule from data to actions}\}\in[0,+\infty].$$
These suprema and infima are taken in the extended order on $\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]]); they exist by
[[lem-extended-reals-complete]]. The parameter set is nonempty and the rule
class is nonempty under the action-space hypothesis, so these are suprema and
infima of nonempty sets of nonnegative extended risks.
A rule is minimax if its worst-case risk equals this infimum. These definitions
make no assertion that a minimizer exists. Nonemptiness of $\mathsf D$ ensures
the rule class is nonempty: fixing any $a_0\in\mathsf D$ gives the constant
point-mass rule $x\mapsto\delta_{a_0}$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in The exponential series converges absolutely for every real argument. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of The factorial $n!$ and the falling factorial $n^{\underline{k}}$, defined by recursion in $\mathbb{N}$, $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing), and powers and series are those of Integer powers $a^m$ and Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series.

This is a real power series centred at $0$ (A real power series about a centre, its interval of convergence, and its radius in $[0,+\infty]$). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

**The factorial.** By the recursion theorem (The recursion theorem) applied to the
set $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$, the starting element $(0,1)$ and the function
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot \sigma(k))$, and by the same induction on the
first coordinate as in Finite sums and finite products of natural numbers, $\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ in $\mathbb{N}$, there is a unique
$F : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with

$$F(0) = 1, \qquad F(\sigma(n)) = F(n)\cdot\sigma(n) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

We write $n! := F(n)$. Thus $0! = 1$, $1! = 0!\cdot 1 = 1$, $2! = 1!\cdot 2 = 2$,
$3! = 6$, $4! = 24$, $5! = 120$, $6! = 720$.

**$0! = 1$ is the base clause of this recursion**, not a convention imported from
elsewhere. Nothing about empty products is presupposed; the agreement with the
empty product is proved below, in clause (a), rather than assumed.

**Truncated difference.** Throughout, $n - k$ is the operation fixed in
Finite sums and finite products of natural numbers, $\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ in $\mathbb{N}$: the unique $j$ with $k + j = n$ when
$k \le n$, and $0$ when $n < k$.

**The falling factorial.** For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ define $n^{\underline{k}}$ by
recursion on $k$, by the recursion theorem applied to
$\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ with starting element $(0,1)$ and
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot (n-k))$:

$$n^{\underline{0}} = 1, \qquad n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k) .$$

So $n^{\underline{1}} = 1\cdot(n-0) = n$ and $n^{\underline{2}} = n\,(n-1)$, and
for $k \le n$ the value is the product $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$ of the $k$ topmost
factors.

**Four facts, proved here because the page uses each of them.**

**(a) The factorial is the product of the first $n$ positive naturals.**
$n! = \prod_{j<n}\sigma(j) = \prod_{j<n}(j+1)$, the $\mathbb{N}$-valued product of
Finite sums and finite products of natural numbers, $\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ in $\mathbb{N}$. Induction (The principle of mathematical induction): at
$n = 0$ both sides are $1$, the empty product and the base clause agreeing; and
$\prod_{j<\sigma(n)}\sigma(j) = \big(\prod_{j<n}\sigma(j)\big)\cdot\sigma(n) = n!\cdot\sigma(n) = \sigma(n)!$.
**So the empty-product reading and the base-clause reading are the same reading**,
and neither was assumed.

**(b) $n! \ne 0$, and $\iota(n!) = \prod^{\mathbb{R}}_{j<n}\iota(j+1)$.** For the
first, $0! = 1 \ne 0$ (The von Neumann naturals form a Peano system) and
$\sigma(n)! = n!\cdot\sigma(n)$ is a product of two nonzero naturals, which is
nonzero: if $xy = 0$ with $y \ne 0$ then $xy = 0\cdot y$
(Zero and one under multiplication) and cancellation gives $x = 0$
(Cancellation for multiplication by a nonzero factor). So $n! \ne 0$ for every $n$ by induction. For the second, apply the bridge clause
6 of that lemma to clause (a) above. This is what makes the factorial of this
page and the real-valued product $\prod_{j<n}(j+1)$ used elsewhere in the library
**one object seen twice**, rather than two unrelated notions.

**(c) $n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$ for $k \le n$.** Induction on $k$, for
all $n$ at once. At $k = 0$ this reads $1 \cdot n! = n!$. Assume it at $k$ and
let $\sigma(k) \le n$; then $k \le n$, and writing $d := n - k$ we have
$k + d = n$ and $d \ne 0$, since $k + 0 = k \ne n$; so $d = \sigma(e)$ for a
unique $e$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor), and $\sigma(k) + e = n$, that is
$e = n - \sigma(k)$ (Addition is cancellative). Therefore
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}}\cdot\big(n-\sigma(k)\big)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)\cdot e! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\big(e!\cdot\sigma(e)\big) = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\sigma(e)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$,
using commutativity and associativity of multiplication
(Multiplication is associative, Multiplication is commutative) and the recursion
clause for the factorial.

**(d) Boundary values.** $n^{\underline{0}} = 1$ for every $n$, by the base
clause; $n^{\underline{n}} = n!$, since clause (c) at $k = n$ gives
$n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0! = n!$ and $0! = 1$; and
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ whenever $k > n$. For the last, $n - n = 0$ gives
$n^{\underline{\sigma(n)}} = n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0 = 0$, the clause
$x \cdot 0 = 0$ being definitional (Multiplication of natural numbers), and if
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ then
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = 0$ as well, so $n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ for every
$k \ge \sigma(n)$ by induction.

Let $F$ be a field (Field) with additive identity $0_F$ and
multiplicative identity $1_F$. Define
$\iota : \mathbb{N} \to F$ by recursion on $\mathbb{N}$
(The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann), The recursion theorem):

$$\iota(0) \;:=\; 0_F, \qquad \iota(n+1) \;:=\; \iota(n) + 1_F .$$

$\iota(n)$ is the **canonical natural** of $n$ in $F$. It is also written
$n \cdot 1_F$, and for $n \ge 1$ it is $1_F$ added to itself $n$ times.

**Why the notation is needed at all.** A natural number in this library is a von
Neumann natural, that is a set (The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)), and a set is not an
element of $F$. So $1/n$, $n^{\alpha}$ and $x/n$ are not expressions of $F$ when
$n$ is a natural: what they mean is $1/\iota(n)$, $\iota(n)^{\alpha}$ and
$x/\iota(n)$. The map $\iota$ is what carries a counting number into the field,
and writing it is the whole reason a reader meets $1/\iota(k+1)$ where an
informal text would write $1/(k+1)$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field, with field structure as in Field, and for
$n \ge 1$ let $n \cdot 1_F$ denote the canonical natural number
$\underbrace{1_F + \cdots + 1_F}_{n}$, defined recursively by $1 \cdot 1_F = 1_F$
and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F = n \cdot 1_F + 1_F$. Then for every $n \ge 1$:

- $n \cdot 1_F > 0$ and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F > n \cdot 1_F$;
- the map $n \mapsto n \cdot 1_F$ is strictly increasing, hence injective, on $\{1, 2, 3, \dots\}$;
- $(m+n) \cdot 1_F = m \cdot 1_F + n \cdot 1_F$ and $(mn) \cdot 1_F = (m \cdot 1_F)(n \cdot 1_F)$ for all $m, n \ge 1$.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$, where $\mathbb{R}$ is the ambient ordered field
(Ordered field, Field).

**Natural exponents.** By the recursion theorem (The recursion theorem) applied to
the set $\mathbb{R}$, the starting element $1$ and the function
$f(x) = x \cdot a$, there is a unique function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$,
written $n \mapsto a^n$, with

$$a^0 = 1, \qquad a^{n+1} = a^n \cdot a \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Thus $a^1 = a$, $a^2 = a \cdot a$, and so on. Note that this is defined for
**every** $a$, including $a = 0$.

**Negative exponents.** If $a \ne 0$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, set

$$a^{-n} := (a^n)^{-1}.$$

**Why that is legitimate.** The right-hand side presupposes that $a^n$ is
invertible, that is, that $a^n \ne 0$. This is a proof obligation and not an
observation, and it is discharged by claim 2 of Laws of integer exponents: for $a \ne 0$
in a field, $a^n \ne 0$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, proved there by induction on
$n$ from the fact that a field has no zero divisors (A field has no zero divisors: $ab = 0 \Rightarrow a = 0$ or $b = 0$).
That lemma is a statement *about* the operation introduced here, so it depends on
this definition and is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its
`deps` (SCHEMA §3). Given $a^n \ne 0$, the value $(a^n)^{-1}$ is a single
well-determined element, because multiplicative inverses in a field are unique
(Identities and inverses in a field are unique).

**Integer exponents.** Every integer $m$ (The integers as equivalence classes of pairs of naturals) is either
$n$ or $-n$ for a unique natural $n$, where $n$ in these integer expressions denotes its image under the
embedding $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ (The naturals embed in the integers,
Arithmetic on the integers). This too is a citation and not a slogan: the order on
$\mathbb{Z}$ is total (The integers form a totally ordered ring), so $m \ge 0$ or $m < 0$; the
image of $\iota$ is exactly the set of nonnegative integers, and each of them is
$n$ for a unique natural $n$ (The naturals embed in the integers); and if $m < 0$ then
$-m > 0$, by compatibility of the order with addition (The integers form a totally ordered ring),
so $-m = n$ and $m = -n$, with $n$ unique because $\iota$ is
injective. The two clauses above therefore define $a^m$ for every
$m \in \mathbb{Z}$ whenever $a \ne 0$, and for every $m \in \mathbb{N}$ for
arbitrary $a$. The two exponent domains are disjoint: the natural clause
handles $m \ge 0$, including $m = 0$, while the negative clause requires
$n \ge 1$ and therefore handles only $m < 0$.

Let $a, b$ be elements of a field ([[def-field]]) and let integer powers be as in
[[def-integer-power]].

1. For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$: $a^{m+n} = a^m a^n$, $(a^m)^n = a^{mn}$ and $(ab)^n = a^n b^n$.
2. If $a \ne 0$ then $a^n \ne 0$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and $a^{-m} = (a^m)^{-1}$ for every $m \in \mathbb{Z}$ ([[def-int-operations]]).
3. If $a \ne 0$ and $b \ne 0$ then all three identities of claim 1 hold for all $m, n \in \mathbb{Z}$.

Let $(x_k)$ and $(y_k)$ be sequences of reals ([[def-sequence]]) converging to
$x$ and $y$ respectively ([[def-real-limit]]). If $x_k \le y_k$ eventually, that
is for all $k$ from some index on, then

$$\lim_{k} x_k \;\le\; \lim_{k} y_k .$$

In particular, if $x_k \ge 0$ eventually then $\lim_k x_k \ge 0$, and if
$a \le x_k \le b$ eventually then $a \le \lim_k x_k \le b$.

The conclusion is **not** strict, and cannot be made strict; see the remarks
below and the false statement at the end of this page.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power (Integer powers $a^m$),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges (Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ and let $\mathcal A=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. If finite measures $\mu$ and $
u$ on $(X,\mathcal A)$ agree on $\mathcal P$ and satisfy $\mu(X)=
u(X)$, then $\mu=
u$ on $\mathcal A$.

The total-mass equality is separate because this library's pi-system convention does not require $X\in\mathcal P$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty. The following are equivalent.

1. $A$ is compact.
2. $A$ is closed and bounded.
3. $A$ is pseudocompact.
4. Every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ attains a maximum and a minimum on $A$.

This theorem is a ZF statement. The nonemptiness hypothesis is necessary for condition 4, because the empty image has neither a maximum nor a minimum.

If $f:X\to Y$ is continuous between topological spaces, then
$f^{-1}[B]\in\mathcal B(X)$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(Y)$.

derivations.claim: If $Q=0$, then $\Theta_a(Q)=\{0\}$. The zero estimator has minimax risk zero, and the $D=0$ cutoff expression is also zero, so the asserted inequalities hold. Hence assume $Q>0$.

Put $\tau_j^2=\epsilon^2s_j^{-2}$ and let $\mathcal C$ be the set of sequences $r_j\ge0$ with $\sum_j a_j^2r_j\le Q^2$. For $r\in\mathcal C$, define $J(r)=\sum_j\min(r_j,\tau_j^2)$. Since $a_j\ge a_1>0$, one has $\sum_jr_j\le Q^2/a_1^2$, so $J(r)$ is finite.

As $s_j\to0$ and $\epsilon>0$, $\tau_j^2\to\infty$. Choose $N\ge1$ so that $\tau_j^2>Q^2/a_1^2$ for $j>N$. Every feasible $r$ then has $r_j<\tau_j^2$ on that tail. Replacing its tail by $\widetilde r_{N+1}=(\sum_{j>N}a_j^2r_j)/a_{N+1}^2$ at coordinate $N+1$ and zero thereafter preserves the weighted budget and does not decrease $J$, because $a_j\ge a_{N+1}$ for $j>N$ and $\sum_{j>N}r_j\le\widetilde r_{N+1}<\tau_{N+1}^2$. The finite-dimensional feasible set in coordinates $1,\ldots,N+1$ is nonempty (it contains zero), closed, and bounded (each coordinate is at most $Q^2/a_j^2$). The finite sum $J$ is continuous there, so [F9] gives a finite-support maximizer $r^*$.

For $k\in\mathbb N$, put $c_k:=(k+3)!$. By induction, $c_k\ge6\cdot3^k$, with strict inequality for $k\ge1$: the base case is $c_0=3!=6$, and if $c_k\ge6\cdot3^k$, then $c_{k+1}=(k+4)c_k\ge4c_k\ge24\cdot3^k>18\cdot3^k=6\cdot3^{k+1}$, using $(k+4)\ge4$ and $c_k>0$. Thus for every $N\ge4$, $$\sum_{n=0}^{N}\frac1{n!}\le\frac52+\frac16\sum_{k=0}^{N-3}3^{-k}-\frac1{72},$$ because the $n=4$ term is strictly below its comparison term by $1/18-1/24=1/72$ and all other terms from $n\ge3$ are bounded by the induction. For $k=0$ one has $(1/3)^0=3^0=1$. For $k\ge1$, the product and reciprocal laws in [F7] give $3^k(1/3)^k=(3(1/3))^k=1$, hence $(1/3)^k=(3^k)^{-1}=3^{-k}$. Applying the geometric-series formula in [F7] at ratio $1/3$ therefore gives $\sum_{k\ge0}3^{-k}=1/(1-1/3)=3/2$. By [F7], the left partial sums tend to $e$ and these geometric sums tend to $3/2$; [F7] therefore gives $e\le\frac{11}{4}-\frac1{72}<\frac{11}{4}$. Hence $2\sqrt{2e}<\sqrt{22}<\frac{121}{25}=(\frac{11}{5})^2$.

The compact-SVD coordinate realization uses Countable Choice [A1]. For each $D$, the first $D$ coordinate evaluations are measurable in the product Borel data space [F1], and their finite-support embedding into $\ell^2$ is continuous; thus the cutoff rule [F3] is measurable, including the constant rule at $D=0$. Its squared loss is measurable by [F10].

Among the finite-support maximizers choose one, $r^*$, with the longest initial saturated segment, and let $D$ be its length; this choice exists because step 1.3 bounds the support by $N+1$. If $P=\{j:r_j^*\ge\tau_j^2\}$ had a later saturated index $j>D+1$, then $i=D+1$ is the first gap before such an index and $r_i^*<\tau_i^2$. Set $\delta=\tau_i^2-r_i^*>0$. Since $s_j$ is nonincreasing, $\tau_i^2\le\tau_j^2$, so $\delta\le\tau_i^2\le\tau_j^2\le r_j^*$. Replacing $r_i^*$ by $r_i^*+\delta$ and $r_j^*$ by $r_j^*-\delta$ does not increase the budget, since $a_i\le a_j$, and does not decrease $J$, since the gain at $i$ is $\delta$ and the loss at $j$ is at most $\delta$. It therefore gives a maximizer whose initial saturated segment has length at least $D+1$, a contradiction. Thus $P=\{1,\ldots,D\}$ for some $D\ge0$.

Let the prior choose independently, for each $j\le N+1$, the two values $\pm b_j$ with equal probability, where $b_j=\min\{\sqrt{r_j^*},\tau_j\}$, and set all later coordinates to zero. Every point in its finite support belongs to $\Theta_a(Q)$ because $\sum_{j\le N+1}a_j^2b_j^2\le\sum_ja_j^2r_j^*\le Q^2$. For any such truth $\eta$, relative to the zero-truth product law $P_0$, the likelihood ratio is $L_\eta(z)=\prod_{j=1}^{N+1}\exp(\eta_jz_j/\tau_j^2-\eta_j^2/(2\tau_j^2))$. For a cylinder determined by a finite coordinate set $F$, split $F$ into active coordinates $F\cap\{1,\ldots,N+1\}$ and inactive coordinates. On each active coordinate, multiplying the zero-mean Gaussian density by its factor in $L_\eta$ gives the shifted Gaussian density; inactive coordinates retain their zero-truth density, and active likelihood factors outside $F$ integrate to one. Finite-coordinate independence therefore gives equality of the two probability measures on every such cylinder, and the product density integrates to one. These cylinders form a generating pi-system, so [F8] gives equality on the full product Borel sigma-algebra and proves that $L_\eta$ is the likelihood ratio for the entire experiment. The finite product prior and this factorized likelihood give a coordinatewise posterior.

The admissible cutoff rule from step 1.5 has minimax risk no greater than its worst-case risk by [F6]. For each $D$ this risk is the exact expression in [F4]; taking the infimum over $D$ gives $R_*(\epsilon)\le R_{\rm cut}(\epsilon)$.

Fix $r\in\mathcal C$ and $m\ge N+1$, and truncate $r$ after coordinate $m$; the truncation remains feasible. The segment from $r^*$ to this finite-support truncation is feasible, and its finite sum $J$ is maximized at its $r^*$ endpoint. Its right derivative there is therefore nonpositive. Since $P=\{1,\ldots,D\}$ by step 2.1, coordinates $j>D$ are strictly below their caps at $r^*$ and contribute their direction increments; coordinates $j\le D$ with $r_j^*>\tau_j^2$ contribute zero, while those with $r_j^*=\tau_j^2$ contribute $\min(r_j-\tau_j^2,0)$. Consequently $\sum_{D<j\le m}(r_j-r_j^*)+\sum_{\{j\le D:r_j^*=\tau_j^2\}}\min(r_j-\tau_j^2,0)\le0$. Letting $m\to\infty$ is legitimate because $\sum r_j$ and $\sum r_j^*$ converge. Rearranging gives $\sum_{j>D}r_j\le\sum_{j>D}r_j^*+\sum_{\{j\le D:r_j^*=\tau_j^2\}}(\tau_j^2-r_j)_+\le\sum_{j>D}r_j^*+\sum_{j=1}^{D}\tau_j^2$.

The randomized rule is a parameter-independent kernel from the data by [F6], so conditioning on its action does not alter the posterior established in step 2.2. For each active coordinate, the conditional squared error is its posterior variance plus a nonnegative squared displacement from the posterior mean. Thus every rule's prior-averaged risk is at least the sum of the scalar Bayes risks. Each scalar prior is supported at $\pm\min\{\sqrt{r_j^*},\tau_j\}$, so [F5] bounds that sum below by $\sum_{j\le N+1}\min(r_j^*,\tau_j^2)/\sqrt{2e}=J_*/\sqrt{2e}$. The supremum risk dominates the supported prior average; taking the minimax infimum gives $R_*(\epsilon)^2\ge J_*/\sqrt{2e}$.

For any $\theta\in\Theta_a(Q)$, the sequence $r_j=\theta_j^2$ belongs to $\mathcal C$. Step 3.1 bounds its omitted squared norm. The cutoff risk is that tail plus the retained variance by [F4], so at the cutoff $D$ from step 2.1 its worst-case risk is at most $\sum_{j>D}r_j^*+2\sum_{j\le D}\tau_j^2\le2J_*$. Therefore $R_{\rm cut}(\epsilon)^2\le2J_*$.
Combining steps 4.1 and 3.2 yields $R_{\rm cut}(\epsilon)^2\le2\sqrt{2e}\,R_*(\epsilon)^2$.
Since both risks are nonnegative, steps 5.1 and 1.4 imply $R_{\rm cut}(\epsilon)\le\frac{11}{5}R_*(\epsilon)$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear operator of infinite rank, viewed as an inverse model with exact datum $Kx$. Here compact means that the image of every bounded subset has compact closure. Write $N(K)=\{x\in X:Kx=0\}$ and $H_0=\overline{\operatorname{ran}K}$. Fix a positive singular system $(s_j,v_j,u_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ for $K$, where $\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$, $s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots>0$, $s_j\to0$, $Kv_j=s_ju_j$, $(v_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $N(K)^\perp$, and $(u_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $H_0$. A complete orthonormal basis is an orthonormal family whose closed linear span is the whole indicated subspace. These are the compact SVD conventions; in particular, this model concerns minimum-norm representatives in $N(K)^\perp$ and does not estimate a kernel component.

For a truth $x\in N(K)^\perp$, let $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$. The complete-basis coefficient map identifies $N(K)^\perp$ bijectively and isometrically with $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, so every $\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ is a model parameter. For $\epsilon>0$, take the functional white-noise experiment on the separable Hilbert space $H_0$ with observations $Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_Y+\epsilon W(g)$, where $W$ is centered, has covariance $\mathbb E[W(g)W(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_Y$, and has independent standard-normal values on every finite orthonormal tuple. The countable complete basis makes $H_0$ separable. Define $\xi_j=W(u_j)$ and $Z_j=Y_x(u_j)/s_j$. The sequence sample space is $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ with the product Borel sigma-algebra, meaning the sigma-algebra generated by its coordinate projections. The coordinate law is the pushforward of the functional experiment under $y\mapsto(y(u_j)/s_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$; this map is measurable because each coordinate is a cylinder evaluation followed by scalar multiplication. The compact SVD expansion gives $\langle Kx,u_j\rangle_Y=s_j\theta_j$, and the positive-noise white-noise coordinate theorem gives the independent standard-normal coordinates $\xi_j$. Hence the normalized coordinates satisfy $Z_j=\theta_j+\epsilon s_j^{-1}\xi_j,\qquad j\in\mathbb N.$

For the zero-noise boundary $\epsilon=0$, define the sequence experiment separately by the point mass at $\theta$, so $Z_j=\theta_j$. This boundary is not an instance of the positive-noise functional experiment.

Let $Q\in[0,\infty)$ and let $a=(a_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ be a nondecreasing sequence of positive real numbers, so $0<a_1\le a_2\le\cdots$. The statistical ellipsoid of radius $Q$ and weights $a$ in the Gaussian sequence inverse model is
$$\Theta_a(Q)=\left\{\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R):\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}a_j^2\theta_j^2\le Q^2\right\}.$$
No assumption that $a_j\to\infty$ is included. In particular, this definition does not assert that the ellipsoid is compact in $\ell^2$.

Assume Countable Choice and let $\epsilon\ge0$. In the Gaussian sequence inverse model with positive singular numbers $(s_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$, let $Q\ge0$ and let $(a_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ be positive and nondecreasing. For each $\theta\in\Theta_a(Q)$, define the squared sequence risk of the cutoff estimator at $D\in\mathbb N_0$ by
$$R_\theta(D):=\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[\|\widehat\theta_D(Z)-\theta\|_{\ell^2}^2\right].$$
Then its exact worst-case squared sequence risk is
$$\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_a(Q)}R_\theta(D)=\frac{Q^2}{a_{D+1}^2}+\epsilon^2\sum_{j=1}^{D}s_j^{-2},$$
where the sum is $0$ for $D=0$. The supremum is attained by the one-coordinate truth $\theta^\star=(Q/a_{D+1})e_{D+1}$, with $\theta^\star=0$ when $Q=0$.

Assume Countable Choice. Fix $\epsilon>0$, $Q\ge0$, a nonincreasing sequence $s_j>0$ with $s_j\to0$, and a nondecreasing sequence $a_j>0$. Observe $Z_j=\theta_j+\epsilon s_j^{-1}\xi_j$ for $j\ge1$, where the $\xi_j$ are independent standard normal variables, and let the unknown parameter range over
$$\Theta_a(Q)=\left\{\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R):\sum_{j\ge1}a_j^2\theta_j^2\le Q^2\right\}.$$
Let $R_*(\epsilon)$ be the square root of the minimax expected squared $\ell^2$ error over all measurable deterministic or randomized estimators from the product Borel data space to $\ell^2$, and put
$$R_{\rm cut}(\epsilon)=\left[\inf_{D\in\mathbb N_0}\left\{\frac{Q^2}{a_{D+1}^2}+\epsilon^2\sum_{j=1}^{D}s_j^{-2}\right\}\right]^{1/2},\qquad\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}.$$
Then $R_*(\epsilon)\le R_{\rm cut}(\epsilon)\le2.2R_*(\epsilon)$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$ states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $a>0$ and $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$a^x:=\exp(x\log a).$$
For the supplementary zero-base convention, define $0^x:=0$ when $x>0$.

The expressions $0^0$ and $0^x$ for $x<0$ are left undefined. Negative bases are not assigned arbitrary real powers.

For $a,b>0$ and $r,s\in\mathbb R$,
$$a^{r+s}=a^ra^s,\qquad (ab)^r=a^rb^r,\qquad (a/b)^r=a^r/b^r,\qquad (a^r)^s=a^{rs}.$$

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power (Integer powers $a^m$),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges (Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ and every real $a>0$,
$$\frac{x^m}{\exp(ax)}\longrightarrow0\qquad(x\to+\infty).$$

For a lower bound, the at least $D/2$ indices with $D/2\le j\le D$ each satisfy $j^q\ge(D/2)^q$, so $\sum_{j=1}^D j^q\ge(D/2)^{q+1}$. Thus $\sum_{j\le D}j^q\asymp D^{q+1}$. Also the finite geometric-sum identity gives $\sum_{j\le D}e^{2pj}\asymp e^{2pD}$ for each fixed $p>0$.

Suppose $s_j\asymp j^{-p}$ and $a_j\asymp j^\kappa$. With $H=\epsilon^{-2/(2\kappa+2p+1)}$ and $D_0=\lfloor H\rfloor$, step 1.1 and [F2] show that both terms of $B_{D_0}$ are $O(H^{-2\kappa})$. For any $D\le D_0$, monotonicity of $a_j$ gives $Q^2/a_{D+1}^2\ge Q^2/a_{D_0+1}^2\asymp H^{-2\kappa}$; for $D>D_0$, the variance is at least $\epsilon^2\sum_{j\le D_0}j^{2p}\asymp\epsilon^2H^{2p+1}=H^{-2\kappa}$. Therefore $\inf_D B_D\asymp H^{-2\kappa}$ and the cutoff RMS error is $\asymp\epsilon^{\kappa/(\kappa+p+1/2)}$.

Suppose $s_j\asymp e^{-pj}$ and $a_j\asymp j^\kappa$. Put $L=\log(1/\epsilon)$ and $D_0=\left\lfloor(L-\kappa\log L)/p\right\rfloor$. By [F7], $\log L/L\to0$, so $D_0\asymp L$. At $D_0$, the squared bias and variance in [F2] are both $O(L^{-2\kappa})$. For $D\le D_0$, the bias is at least $Q^2/a_{D_0+1}^2\asymp L^{-2\kappa}$; for $D>D_0$, the geometric variance is at least $\epsilon^2e^{2pD_0}\asymp e^{-2L}e^{2L}L^{-2\kappa}=L^{-2\kappa}$. Hence $\inf_D B_D\asymp L^{-2\kappa}$ and the cutoff RMS error is $\asymp L^{-\kappa}$.

Suppose $s_j\asymp j^{-p}$ and $a_j\asymp e^{\kappa j}$. Put $L=\log(1/\epsilon)$ and $D_0=\left\lfloor(L-(p+\tfrac12)\log L)/\kappa\right\rfloor$. Again [F7] gives $D_0\asymp L$. At $D_0$, the squared bias and variance are both $O(\epsilon^2L^{2p+1})$. For $D\le D_0$, monotonicity of $a_j$ gives bias at least $Q^2/a_{D_0+1}^2\asymp e^{-2\kappa D_0}\asymp\epsilon^2L^{2p+1}$; for $D>D_0$, the polynomial variance is at least $\epsilon^2\sum_{j\le D_0}j^{2p}\asymp\epsilon^2L^{2p+1}$. Thus $\inf_D B_D\asymp\epsilon^2L^{2p+1}$ and the cutoff RMS error is $\asymp\epsilon L^{p+1/2}$.

Suppose $s_j\asymp e^{-pj}$ and $a_j\asymp e^{\kappa j}$. Let $L=\log(1/\epsilon)$ and $D_0=\lfloor L/(p+\kappa)\rfloor$. Then $D_0\to\infty$; at this cutoff the squared bias and geometric variance are both $O(\epsilon^{2\kappa/(p+\kappa)})$. For $D\le D_0$, monotonicity of $a_j$ gives bias at least $Q^2/a_{D_0+1}^2\asymp e^{-2\kappa D_0}\asymp\epsilon^{2\kappa/(p+\kappa)}$; for $D>D_0$, the variance is at least $\epsilon^2e^{2pD_0}\asymp\epsilon^{2\kappa/(p+\kappa)}$. Hence $\inf_D B_D\asymp\epsilon^{2\kappa/(p+\kappa)}$ and the cutoff RMS error is $\asymp\epsilon^{\kappa/(p+\kappa)}$.

Steps 2.1–2.4 establish the four rates for $(\inf_D B_D)^{1/2}$. By [A1], the compact singular-system coordinate model and its minimax comparison theorem are used under Countable Choice. By [F3], this quantity and the minimax RMS error differ by at most the fixed factor $2.2$, so the same four order-sharp rates hold for $R_*(\epsilon)$.
